owner: W1-17. The layer every settlement's local answers hang off. RI-DLG01 §A: a topic exists ONCE, engine-wide; a hundred NPCs may have a hundred different answers to it.

infos.x: Nine hundred on paper. Four hundred standing. The rest is rot, fever and the muster board. We hold the roads. That is all we hold.

The Ninth was raised for the Arnesian War and never stood down, which in Imperial practice means it was never funded again either. Its establishment is a document from the reign of a dead emperor and its actual strength is whatever the tribune can be persuaded to admit to in a given year.
They are not unkind, the soldiers, they are only very tired and very wet, and a tired wet man will move you along without malice in a way that a rested dry one somehow never manages.
Soldiers buy. Soldiers do not pay. Friend, this one keeps two prices.
Tribune Ancus Varo. Twelve years in post. He is not sent for and he sends for none. Draw your own conclusion, citizen.

The tribune's appointment is renewed by the silence of the Provincial Office, which is technically a valid mechanism and is generally understood to mean that no one in Cyrodiil can remember why the post exists.
The tribune. Old. Fair. Will not spend a man he cannot replace. Ask him yourself. He is in the wall house at Stormhold.
Were Varo a worse man he would be a richer one, and were he a better one he would have reported the muster years ago. He is precisely as honest as a man can be while remaining in post.
Names, ranks, watches. Nailed by the gate. Read it and you know the garrison. Most people never read it.

The interesting property of a muster board is that it is a public document that is never audited, and the interesting property of the Ninth's board is that a number of the names on it have been there without interruption since before the fever year, which is longer than anyone actually serves.
You did not hear it from me. Twenty-one names on that board are dead. The pay still goes out. The pay is signed for. I am not asking who.

The discrepancy is arithmetical and therefore not deniable: the ration returns and the pay returns disagree by twenty-one men over four years, and rations are drawn by people who eat while pay is drawn by whoever holds the chit.
Quaestor Belena Sarn. Keeps the chest. Keeps the ledger. Keeps her own counsel. Careful, citizen.

Sarn came out with the last honest posting the Office made and has been here since, which is either a testament to her patience or evidence of something she cannot afford to leave behind. The catalogue does not distinguish between those two states and neither, generally, does anyone else.
The pay woman buys nothing. Friend, buying nothing is not a thing people do. This one watches her.

The Office is the Empire's memory of Argonia, and it is a bad one. It surveys, it taxes, it issues charters, and it does all three on the assumption that the province is a version of Cyrodiil that has been rained on. The single most consequential document it holds is a treaty it has not opened in ninety years.
The Office. Yes. If you have a grievance, provincial, they will record it beautifully.
Clerks. They pay us. Late. Every quarter. Never enough.

A charter is the Empire's way of saying that a thing which existed before it arrived now exists because of it. Thorn has one, and it is genuine, and it is the only reason there is still a king in that hall.
Paper. Presumably you have seen paper before.

Three years behind, and the years it is behind are the fever year and the two after it, which is exactly the period a person would want if they intended to look up who died and who inherited. I mention this because I have been asked for those years four times this season and by four people who did not know each other.
Everything off a boat goes on it. Weight, owner, port. Sign it or lose it. Simple.
A manifest is a story about a cart. Friend, this one tells good stories.
Sap weighs heavy wet. The Ledger buys wet, sells dry. Friend, the difference is a cart in ten. It is not weighed twice.
The practice is not fraud in the legal sense, because no weight is misstated; the fraud, if that is the word, is in the interval between the two weighings, and the interval is weather.
Sap out of a well. Bone out of a xanmeer. Anything with a rootkeeper's mark. Carry it and you are ours.
Contraband is only cargo with an opinion about it. Friend, this one has opinions too.
Fine first. Then the cell. Then the prison at Blackrose. Do not reach the third one, citizen.

The Empire fines and the interior does not, and the reason is not mercy: a fine is a thing that ends, and what is owed to a family for a death is not a thing that ends, it is a thing that is carried until it is put down by agreement.

A death is owed to the kin, not to the province, and it is settled between them, and no writ from any office in Cyrodiil extinguishes it, though a ruling from an arbiter of ours will, which is why the arbiters are hunted and why they are protected.
Their law. Not ours. It still gets people killed. Watch yourself in the interior, citizen.

A ku-vastei hears what was done and says what is now true, and once it has been said the matter is closed and the family that was owed will not pursue it, because to pursue it after a ruling is itself a debt.

The Order is attested in Imperial records only as a category of exemption, which is a remarkable thing to find in a tax document: a class of person the Empire agreed in writing not to ask about, in exchange for a peace it has never publicly admitted needing.
They are given at the sign and raised apart and they do what is required, supplicant, and the covenant does not pretend it is clean; it says only that it is owed.
Stories. Assassins under the boards. I have been here nine years. I have not seen one.

A well is a place where a root has come near enough to the surface that what it makes can be taken without cutting, and it is tended because a thing that gives without being cut is owed a great deal more than a thing that is harvested.
Wells make sap. Sap makes coin. Friend, this one is not permitted near them. This one manages.

The Office classifies a sapwell as a mineral asset, which is the single funniest sentence in the provincial register and has caused more actual violence than any other administrative decision made in this province.
It is not a medicine and it is not a drink. It is the tree deciding something about you, supplicant, and it is not always kind, and it is never quick, and it is never sold.
Small jar. Big price. Friend, this one does not ask what it does.
If you are asking whether it can be shipped, provincial, the answer is that it has been, at scale, for two centuries, and that the price reflects what happens to the people who ship it.
The one at Helstrom is the oldest that still speaks, and Helstrom is not a city that was built beside it but a city that was allowed inside it, and the difference is the whole of what we are.

Every attested account agrees the tree predates the settlement and none agrees by how much, with the estimates in the chronology ranging across a factor of nine, which is generally a sign that the question is being answered by people who need a particular answer.

Fourteen wells have gone quiet in my lifetime and not one of them was cut, supplicant, which is the part that does not get repeated: it is not the cutters who are killing them, or not only, and I would rather it were.
Quiet well, no sap, no coin. Friend, this one has lost three routes.

They say the wells are going quiet and they say it like it is weather, dry-one, but I slept by the one at Soulrest for six years and I can tell you it did not go quiet all at once, it went quiet the way a person does.

They are all having them on the boards and none will say so first, dry-one, and it is always the same one, and it is always a person standing in water that is warmer than water should be, and I would not mind so much if I did not wake up glad.
The keepers dream now, which we did not, and the dreams come from the direction of the wells that have stopped, and I have written this down four times and burned it three.
Fever dreams. Half the barracks has them. Physician says damp. I say damp too.

What is taken is returned, what is named is kept, and what is owed is carried. It is three sentences long and it has held for longer than the Empire has been able to write, and it is not a religion, supplicant, whatever the chapel tells you.

The Imperial position is that the covenant is a folk religion, and the provincial position among people who have actually lived here is that it is a body of property law with a tree at the top of it, and the second reading explains far more of the litigation.

A hatchling is given a name at the well and it is a description, not a decoration, and it is expected to stop being true, at which point another is given and the first is not forgotten but is not used.
The practice makes the census unusable, which is the second reason the Office's population figures for the interior are wrong; the first is that the Office has never been to the interior.
This one has had four names. Friend, you may use any of them.

It is spoken where it is understood and it is not taught to those who would write it down, supplicant, and the reason is not secrecy but that a written word cannot be taken back and a great many of ours are meant to be.

Four Imperial attempts at a grammar survive and all four contradict each other on the tense system, which suggests either that the language has none or that it has one the surveyors could not hear, and I incline to the second on the evidence of how much trouble they had with the word for river.

Signed after the Arnesian War by an Argonian party the Empire has never fully identified and has never been able to say did not exist. It ended the raiding, it fixed the border, it exempted a category of person from imperial inquiry, and it contains a clause about inheritance that has not been read since the year it was sealed.
The treaty is why my estate is not an estate. Should you find that funny, provincial, you would be in company.
It is a paper about a promise that was not made in a language that has papers, and it has been kept anyway, which says more about the keeping than the paper.
Clause eleven. If a chartered holding has no heir the holding reverts, not to the Empire, but to the well that witnessed the charter. Ninety years and no one has tested it. I intend to.

There is a clause in the treaty that has been transcribed wrongly in every subsequent copy, and the original in the Office annexe at Gideon reads, so far as I can make it out, as a reversion to a place rather than to a person, which is not a thing Imperial law can do and is exactly the thing this province keeps doing to it.

Argonians rose against House Dres and against the slavers generally, and burned a good deal of the border, and were called savages for it in every account written by the people who had been holding them. The war is a hundred and eighty years old and the Ninth Cohort exists because of it and House Dres is still here because of it.
A rebellion, provincial, which was suppressed, and after which everything continued much as before with a treaty on top of it.
It is not a war in our telling, supplicant, it is a return, and the difference is that a war is fought against someone and a return is only walked.

The old road north still has the posts in it, dry-one, every forty paces the whole way to the border, and they have not been pulled up because pulling them up would be a thing that had to be decided by an office.
A road. If you are hoping I will apologise for a road, provincial, you have misjudged the conversation.
Six estates, four factors, one magister and a treaty that says none of it is ours. We remain because leaving would concede the point. Presumably that strikes you as absurd.
They took from the wells and from the families for three hundred years and they are still here, and the covenant says what is owed is carried, so it is carried.
Dres pay well. Dres pay late. Friend, this one still goes.
Not our jurisdiction. Their estates, their law. We do not go in.
I am he, if you were hoping for someone else. Were there a better magister available the House would have sent one thirty years ago.
The old Dunmer at the north estate. Buys books. Pays in silver. Friend, that is all this one knows.
They lend, they buy, they forget a manifest. Friend, they are not thieves. Thieves take once.

The Ledger is a commercial house that happens to own the report chain, which is a more durable arrangement than owning the goods, and it is the only institution in the province that has never once failed to know what a boat was carrying.
We know. We cannot prove it. Every quarter the same.
Each town has one. Quiet room, good chair, bad news. Friend, ask for the ledgerman.
He does not raise his voice and he does not need to, dry-one, and I have watched three men go into that room angry and come out arranging to pay for the privilege.
Not the Ledger. Not near the Ledger. Friend, do not put those two words in one sentence in a room.

They are the ones who were here before the Ledger and they have not agreed to stop being here, and if you want to know the difference, dry-one, the Ledger will ruin you and the Court will simply not have you found.
Sap, bone, egg, hide, and things this one does not name. Lilmoth, low tide, under the second stair. Friend, do not go alone.

What is sold there is taken from wells and from bodies and from nests, supplicant, and every one of those is a thing the covenant says is returned, and the market exists because the Empire's law has no word for the offence.
A guild in the way a flock is a guild. This one pays dues. This one gets a route. Friend, that is the whole society.

They call themselves cutters as though the cutting were the difficulty. The difficulty is that a well which is cut does not stop giving at once, and so the harm is not visible until the cutter is three towns away and cannot be shown it.
Jeel runs the cart between three towns and buys anything. Friend, do not sell to Jeel first. Sell to Jeel second.
Known to us. Nothing proven. Yet.
Boards where there is water. Stone where the Empire could be bothered. Friend, the stone runs out at Gideon.
We patrol three. There are nine. Do the sum, citizen.

There was a proper Imperial road south of the Clay Moor and the marsh has had it back, dry-one, and you can still walk it at the low tide of the year if you know where it goes under, and people do, and some of them come out the other side.

The southern trunk road is carried on the survey as extant, which is administratively true and physically false, and the discrepancy has never been corrected because correcting it would require a man to go and look.

The boards are the province, dry-one, whatever the maps say, because everything that matters here happens on a plank two hands wide with water under it and a man coming the other way who will not give ground.
Walk the boards. Not the ground. Friend, this one has said it twice now.
Keep left. Give way to a laden man. It is not courtesy. It is the fine.
What the tide takes has no owner. What is above the line has one. That is the whole of it. Learn the line.

The doctrine is Imperial in form and entirely native in substance: possession lapses at the high-water mark, which in a province where the high-water mark moves is less a rule of property than an annual redistribution with a legal vocabulary attached.
Everything is ownerless twice a day. Friend, this one owns a very good boat.

Step pyramids, pre-Imperial, and older than the settlements around them by an interval the chronology does not attempt. They are not tombs, whatever the sale catalogues say; the interior arrangement is wrong for it, and the Office knows this and has never issued a correction because the correction would depress a market it taxes.

They were built when the wells were many and they are entered now only by the people who sell what is in them, supplicant, and every one of those people is carrying a debt they have not been told about.
There is one out past the ford with the top off it and I would not sleep in it for any money, dry-one, and I have slept in a great many places you would not.

There are three chronologies of this province in general use and they disagree by four hundred years at the Arnesian War, which is impossible, and the resolution is that one of them is counting from a different event and has never said which. I have spent twenty years on that question and I am now reasonably confident that the event is a flood.

The eastern survey stops mid-sheet. The stated cause is weather. The surveyor's own note on the reverse says the party was ordered to withdraw by a man whose name has since been cut out of the paper with a knife, and the sheet is still in the annexe at Gideon, and it has not been asked for but by me.
Surveyors went east. Came back short. Before my time.

Four years back, and it took the boards first because we are wet and thin, dry-one, and then it went up the hill and took the ones with the dry beds, and that was the only time in my life I have been treated as though we were the same thing.

The mortality is not recorded because the recording apparatus was itself among the mortality, which is a sentence I have written in a report and been asked to remove. The catalogue's gap begins in that year and it is not a coincidence.
The wells were asked for more than they had and three of them stopped, and it has never been said aloud that the two things are one thing, supplicant, but it has been thought.
One per garrison. Overworked. Ours is good. Ours drinks.
The chapel ones will see you if you are quiet and the Imperial ones will see you if you are paying, dry-one, and the bone-setter at Soulrest will see all comers and that is why she has nothing.

The claim rests on conquest that did not occur, cession that was never signed, and a treaty that carefully does not use the word province. It is nonetheless entirely effective, because a claim is a thing that is administered rather than a thing that is true.
They are here, supplicant, and they will not always be here, and what the covenant asks is only that we do not become them while we wait.

The name of the province is a lie of convenience: there is marsh, certainly, but there is also mountain at the Valus, arid rock in the west, petrified forest in the middle, jungle at Blackwood and a red littoral on the eastern coast. A traveller who expects swamp will spend a week being wrong in six different climates.
Thirteen names. Nine roads. Friend, this one has walked nine.

Petrified growth standing where a living forest stood, and standing in the same arrangement, which is the detail that makes the Imperial explanation of gradual mineralisation difficult to hold: gradual processes do not preserve a canopy. Helstrom is inside it, which is presumably not an accident.
Those were trees that did not agree to stop, supplicant, and they are not dead, they are only very slow, and it is not permitted to cut them for exactly that reason.
Dry uplands. Hard cart, good road. Friend, no water for a day. Carry it.
I went up on the moor the summer of the fever because a wet chest does not kill on the Clay Moor, dry-one, and I nearly died of thirst instead, which the province thought was funny.

Unfinished on every map I have handled, and the unfinished portions are not the same on any two of them, which means either that three surveys stopped at three different points or that one survey stopped and two subsequent draughtsmen guessed differently about where.
We do not patrol east of the ford. Orders. Old orders. The why is not asked.

The interior is not empty and it is not lawless, supplicant, it is simply governed by people who did not ask the Empire and will not, and a stranger who walks in without being brought in has made himself a question that will have to be answered.
In there we are a rumour. Go if you must. Go with a guide.
Were the interior worth holding, provincial, it would have been held. It is not. That is the entire strategic history of this province in one sentence.

They kept what the coast put down and they are not gentle about the difference, and if you go among them you will be measured against a covenant you have not read and found short, and that will be survivable if you are quiet.
This one does not trade past the second ford. Friend, this one likes this one's hands.
Dry. Hard. Ours. Stormhold sits on it. Best posting in the province, citizen, which tells you about the province.

Genuine jungle, canopy closed, and the only part of the province where Imperial agriculture has actually worked, which is why Gideon is there and why Gideon is insufferable. The Company takes its name from it and does not operate in it.
Mercenaries. Paid better than us. Do less. Ask their recruiter, not me.
Useful, if you are content to pay for enthusiasm rather than competence. The House retains them and the House does not discuss why.
Crossing on the Helstrom leg. Deep at the turn. Friend, wait for the boards to show.
They call it weeping because of the sound the water makes on the stones, which is not true, dry-one, it is called that because of what the crossing used to be for and it has been agreed to forget.

The channel behind the warehouses at Lilmoth, dry-one, and things come out of it that went in somewhere else entirely, and the Cohort fishes them out and writes drowned and all are satisfied except the ones who watched.
Bad water. Bad district. Four this year. All drowned.

He walked down on his own feet with a man behind him not hurrying, and that is not a drowning however it is written up, and I have told three people and two of them told me to be quieter and the third asked me where I sleep.
One of the four. Nothing on him. Case closed, citizen.
The Ledger's man at Lilmoth. Never leaves the room. Friend, everything in that quarter goes past his chair.

It is a day east of the ford and it is not on any roll and it has not gone quiet, and the keeper who found it kept it off the rolls, and I have never decided whether she was protecting it from the cutters or from us.
Arms, boots, oil. Requisition only. No, not for you. Not without a chit.
Two drakes on a cart. Nothing on a person. Anyone charging you more is stealing.
Two drakes on the book. Five in the hand. Friend, this one pays the two.
The chapel's roll of the tithed, which in Gideon is very nearly the roll of the respectable, and the two names on it that surprise a reader are the two worth asking about.

A proper chapel, stone, with a bell that was carried here in pieces, and a priest who has been quietly conducting the covenant's rites in the vestry for a dozen years on the entirely reasonable grounds that the people asking for them are his parish.

The priest at Gideon is not a fool and is not a traitor to his order, supplicant; he has simply understood that a well and an altar are asked for by the same people at the same hours for the same reasons.
Thornwood. Straight grain. Dunmer buy it for bows. Friend, the Empire buys it for spears.
It is called a forest and it is a field of spikes as tall as a hall, dry-one, and there is one path through it that all of Thorn knows and no map has.
Tide-lichen, boiled. Comes out imperial purple. Friend, the Empire pays for the colour of its own gowns.
The vats take a season off your hands and ten years off your lungs, dry-one, and the yard pays a wage that is very slightly better than the alternative, which is how a yard like that stays full.

The colour is lichen and the lichen is seasonal, so the coast is red for four months and grey for eight, and every Imperial painting of it was made in the four. The Office's revenue projections were also made in the four.
It stopped in my mother's time and the village has stayed, which is not stubbornness, supplicant, it is that a well that has stopped is still owed the tending and the tending falls to them.
They still walk down to it at the tide-turn, dry-one, all of them, and stand there, and go home, and they have not been told to stop and none would dare.
Imperial. Long sentences. Full. Do not end up in it, citizen.

The prison is the largest Imperial structure in the province and its population is recorded to the individual, which makes it the only place in Argonia where the Empire genuinely knows how many people there are.
Half of Blackrose has kin in it and the other half works in it, dry-one, and at the end of a shift they drink together, which I have always found to be the strangest thing in this province.
Old Imperial stone. Sunk to the first windows. Friend, people still live in the second.

Two cities occupying the same plan at different elevations, the lower one Imperial and submerged and the upper one native and built on top of it, which is either a metaphor or the plainest statement of the province's history available to a person standing in a boat.
